replacement: He was only twenty. His brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, and their eldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic. I may as well state my whole opinion at the outset. He was simply a lover of humanity from early on. He took up the monastic life only because, at that time, it struck him as the ideal way out for his soul, which was struggling up from the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. It struck him that way because he believed he had found in the monastery an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, and he had attached himself to Zossima with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. I don’t deny that he was very strange even then, and had been since the cradle. I have mentioned already that he lost his mother in his fourth year, yet remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, “as though she stood living before me.” Such memories can reach back, as everyone knows, even to the age of two. But they seldom last a whole lifetime as isolated spots of light in the darkness, like the one corner left of a huge picture that has faded and vanished everywhere else. That is how it was with him. He remembered a still summer evening and an open window, with the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all). In a corner of the room was the holy image with a lighted lamp before it, and on her knees in front of the image was his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying and moaning. She snatched him up in both arms and squeezed him so tight it hurt, and prayed for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms toward the image as if to place him under the Mother’s protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him away from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother’s face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied but beautiful, as he remembered it. He rarely wanted to speak of this memory to anyone, though. As a child and a youth he was far from outgoing, and he talked very little. That was not from shyness or a sullen dislike of company. It was from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, wholly his own and having nothing to do with other people, yet so important to him that it made him seem to forget them. But he was fond of people. All his life he seemed to trust people completely, and still no one ever thought him a simpleton or naïve. Something about him made you feel at once (and this held true all his life) that he had no wish to sit in judgment on others—that he would never presume to criticize, and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the least condemnation, although he often grieved bitterly. So thoroughly was this so, that even in his earliest youth nothing could surprise or frighten him. At twenty he came to his father’s house, a perfect sink of filthy debauchery. Chaste and pure as he was, he simply withdrew in silence whenever the sight became unbearable, and he showed no sign of contempt or condemnation. His father had once lived as a dependent himself, so he was touchy and quick to take offense, and he received Alyosha at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn’t say much,” he would say, “and he thinks the more.” But soon—within two weeks, in fact—he was embracing and kissing Alyosha terribly often, with drunken tears and sottish sentimentality. Still, he plainly felt a real and deep affection for him, the like of which he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and that had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, who came to look on him quite as their own child. Yet he went to live there at such a tender age that he could not have been calculating or scheming to win affection. The gift of making himself loved immediately and unconsciously was simply inborn in him, part of his nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes ridicule, and even dislike. He was dreamy, for example, and rather solitary. From his earliest years he loved to creep into a corner and read, and yet he was a general favorite all the time he was at school. He was seldom playful or merry, but you could see at a glance that this was not sullenness. On the contrary, he was cheerful and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his schoolmates. Perhaps for that reason, he was afraid of no one, yet the boys realized at once that he took no pride in his fearlessness and seemed not to know he was bold and brave. He never resented an insult. An hour after being wronged, he might speak to the one who had done it, or answer his question, with a look as trusting and open as if nothing had passed between them. It was not that he seemed to have forgotten the insult, or made up his mind to forgive it. He simply did not count it as an insult, and this completely won over the boys and captivated them. He had one trait that made all his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to mock him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. That trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He could not stand to hear certain words and certain talk about women. Unhappily, there are “certain” words and talk that no one can stamp out in schools. Boys who are pure in mind and heart, hardly more than children, love to discuss among themselves, and even out loud, things and pictures and images that even soldiers would think twice about mentioning. More than that, much that soldiers know nothing of is familiar to quite small children of our educated and upper classes. It isn’t moral depravity, or any real inner corruption and cynicism, but it has the look of those, and among the boys it is often considered refined, subtle, daring, and worth copying. When they saw Alyosha Karamazov stick his fingers in his ears whenever they talked of “that,” they would sometimes crowd around him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears. He would struggle, slip down onto the floor, and try to hide, without saying one word of abuse, and endure their insults in silence. In the end, though, they left him alone and stopped teasing him as a “regular girl.” What’s more, they came to view it with pity, as a weakness. In class he was always among the best, but never first.

Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. Quite the opposite: at this time Alyosha was a sturdy, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, glowing with health. He was very handsome, too. He was graceful and moderately tall, with dark brown hair and a regular, rather long, oval face. His dark gray eyes were wide-set and shining. He was very thoughtful and seemed very serene. I will be told, perhaps, that red cheeks do not rule out fanaticism and mysticism. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles are never a stumbling block to a realist. It is not miracles that lead realists to belief. The true realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and ability to disbelieve in the miraculous. Faced with a miracle as an undeniable fact, he would sooner doubt his own senses than accept it. And if he does accept it, he accepts it as a fact of nature that he had simply not recognized before. In the realist, faith does not spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once a realist believes, his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous too. The Apostle Thomas said he would not believe until he saw, but when he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not. He believed only because he wanted to believe, and perhaps in his secret heart he fully believed even when he said, “I do not believe till I see.”

I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, that he had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He chose this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination, and it offered his soul an ideal escape from darkness into light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a young man of our last epoch. That is, he was honest by nature. He wanted the truth, sought it and believed in it, and wanted to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul. He looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. Unfortunately, these young men fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices, and that to sacrifice, for instance, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal, is a sacrifice utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question. It is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”
